beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Run it; don't wait for certainty.
beats.got: Agent output can't tell you if the agent is safe, so you run a check and accept it won't be perfect.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new; a reading list, and I didn't read it

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain) and a plain access review
beats.got: There's a named list of agent risks. I only half know it, so I'd like the list.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: nothing new; my answer would be 'mostly the confluence connection'

beats.trigger: Each tool has a name, a description and an input format.
beats.got: nothing new; I use tool calls daily. I pasted the prompts and skipped reading the answers.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: Nobody can fully certify agent systems, and that doesn't go away.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: nothing new; this is the setup for the next slide

beats.trigger: One passing test is one sample.
beats.got: My 'it looked fine' is a single sample from a non-deterministic system, so it's weak evidence.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five named mitigations. I use scope and review by instinct, and I never thought of split by trust level.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer. Closing it takes evidence, not a better guess.
beats.got: You're allowed to write down 'unknown' as a result. That is more honest than what I normally do.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: I've spent months giving agents more access. Making the failure smaller is the other half, and I never did it.

beats.trigger: Should the agent read from that mailbox? If not, don't connect it.
beats.got: My confluence plan is exactly a door I'd open because I can, not because anyone needs it.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a recap with a pep talk

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: I already write skills. The new part is using one as a security reviewer I can rerun.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The raw run shows which rules an agent can check from files and which it can't. I hadn't separated those.

beats.trigger: Skip studying the policy files first.
beats.got: I tell the agent what matters and it does the policy reading. That's quick, and I like skipping the reading.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: The agent interviews me and builds a two-lens skill. It's my kind of exercise because I can keep extending it.

beats.trigger: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."
beats.got: When the questions get tedious I can hand the choice back and say what I can't control. I'll use that line again.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: nothing new; I save skills all the time

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The skill does not replace the company's own controls.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: I'm not looking for a pass here. I'm running the loop once.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a slash command

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit flagged things in my module-3 system I'd called fine, and it gave me 'can't tell' on some.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The ranked risk list made me uneasy, and the module says to treat that as the signal.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: You apply a fix, reread the residual, and write it down instead of chasing zero.

beats.trigger: Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.
beats.got: nothing new; escalate with evidence to legal or security

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: I've been calling prototypes production. The difference is doing this for every risk, and I did it for one.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: The skill carries across agents and the report holds the decisions.

beats.trigger: *"That rule wasn't ambiguous, I just didn't have the evidence"*
beats.got: The agent writes rules into the root instructions file and I push back where it's vague. Fine, but I would have let it through.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Sharing a skill with a teammate doesn't make anyone own it. That hits my sales-team plan: who maintains it?

beats.trigger: Well-formed English is the attack surface, even via sources.
beats.got: nothing new beyond a recap; the injection point is the one I'd forget

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework with a nudge. I'll probably write them in the room.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two cases about no check on agent output, which fits my misconception, but I won't read them tonight.

take_homes: One 'it looked fine' is a single sample from a non-deterministic system, so I can't use it as evidence the agent is safe.
The cheapest mitigation is not connecting the door, and I should ask who needs confluence access before I wire it in.
A saved agent-audit skill with a policy lens and an agent-risk lens, plus a written residual risk, is something I can rerun on every agent.

monday.move: Run /agent-audit on the sales-team setup I'm building and decide whether the confluence connection stays in.
monday.who: me, then the head of sales for the 'who needs this' question
monday.when: Monday morning before I extend it
monday.stop_condition: I have a written residual-risk line and a named owner, or I cut the confluence connection
monday.blocker: Nobody in sales asked for it and nobody has agreed to maintain it.

misconception.why: 'One passing test is one sample' hit my 'if it looks fine it is fine'. The audit finding things I'd called fine backed it up. I still think reviewing every output is for beginners, but I accept now that checking the system matters.

one_line: the first half is stuff I knew, but the audit found things in my own setup and the 'don't open the door' slide stuck with me.
